What do we want to use as our convergence metric
when comparing BUGS, etc. and Stan?

On 5/16/12 8:24 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> I recommend running until R.hat< 1.1 and ESS> 40 for every parameter.

I've misunderstood answers before, so please
bear with me while I ask the question in a multiple
choice format:

QUESTION: Do we want to monitor for R-hat,
a. the convergence of each parameter (X),
b. the convergence of each parameter squared (X^2), or
c. both of the above?

I believe Matt was arguing for (c) because X might have
a high R-hat without X^2 having a high R-hat. But then
that opens a whole can of worms about monitoring R-hat of
other things like 95% or 50% quantiles.

I'd just as soon not have to do X^2 because it's more
work. But if it's the right thing to do, we should do it.

The R.hat and ESS targets are suggestions for users,
at least until we get all the auto-restart in place and
can have an autorun feature.

> In Jiqiang's plot() function in R, I recommend using colors for R.hat (e.g., yellow for R.hat> 1.1 and red for
R.hat> 1.5). I can't think of a natural way to display ESS but perhaps you'll have an idea.

Again, just to confirm here:

a. variable names in black(?), yellow, red by r-hat,
(discrete not some kind of continuous fade representation)

b. intervals/medians colored by chain, with all chains
displayed as in R2WinBUGS

We'll have to see if yellow has enough contrast -- it might
in ggplot2.

- Bob

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] second moment ESS, etc.?
parts:
The reason for wanting to look at second moments is that HMC can
produce anticorrelated samples, which aren't actually that reliable,
but produce great ESS and R-hat statistics. This shouldn't be a
problem for NUTS, though, since trajectory lengths aren't fixed.

Unfortunately, raw second moments have their own problems. Ideally
we'd be able to easily monitor second central moments (i.e.,
(X-E[X])^2), rather than just X^2, since
E[X^2] = Var[X] + E[X]^2
which is often dominated by E[X]^2, in which case monitoring E[X^2]
isn't much different than monitoring E[X]. But monitoring (X-E[X])^2
is more complicated, since you need an estimate of E[X].

I say we ignore X^2 for now—it's kind of a pain to deal with, and I
think it's mostly a concern when you're using HMC with a fixed number
of steps.

Matt

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] second moment ESS, etc.?
parts:
The other option is to consider the set of monitoring variables as separate from the parameters.  It defaults to the parameters (X), but can be set to an arbitrary function F(X) so that people who are interested in estimating specific functional expectations could set it to something else.  E.G., someone may be interested in the expected data log likelihood, so it makes more sense to monitor that instead of the variables themselves.

Plus, it's easy to come up with distributions (e.g., the parameters of a mixture model, or most anything with exchangeable parameters) where monitoring X will make all the chains look really horrible even if they're doing fine.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] second moment ESS, etc.?
parts:
On 5/18/12 11:22 AM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> The other option is to consider the set of monitoring variables as separate from the parameters.

The notion of "parameter" here is pretty general,
following the BUGS usage. For instance, the
unnormalized log probability is a "parameter"
as is the number of leapfrog steps used by NUTS
per sample. Then the generated quantities and
transformed parameters are also treated like
parameters.

So it's actually easy to add other quantities
on the Stan side as derived quantities.

For instance, if we have

parameters {
real mu;
real(0,) sigma;
}
...
generated quantities {
real(0,) mu_sq;
real(0,) sigma_sq;
mu_sq <- square(mu);
sigma_sq <- square(sigma);
}

then you could monitor mu squared and sigma squared
as parameters.

But this is a bit of a hack. There's really no
reason other than convenience to store the squares
for this.

> It defaults to the
> parameters (X), but can be set to an arbitrary function F(X) so that people who are interested in estimating specific
> functional expectations could set it to something else. E.G., someone may be interested in the expected data log
> likelihood, so it makes more sense to monitor that instead of the variables themselves.
>
> Plus, it's easy to come up with distributions (e.g., the parameters of a mixture model, or most anything with
> exchangeable parameters) where monitoring X will make all the chains look really horrible even if they're doing fine.

We're still partly talking about what the R package
is going to do by default with the analyses. I'm
trying to pin down the minimum we have to do to
prioritize working on that so we can release the R interface.

But I want to make the design as flexible as possible.

I just wrote the visitor functions so you'll be able to
plug in arbitrary functors on the C++ side. And
there won't be any intermediate copying.

The Boost accumulators framework is just a particular
kind of visitor/callback pattern. The accumulator
implements a functor that overrides

operator()(T x)

where T is the scalar type. The built-in ones do things
like calculate means and variances online or buffer
some data to calculate quantiles.

For something like data log likelihood, you'd have to
build it into the generated quantities somehow or
calculate it yourself -- it's not isolated in the
Stan models the way it can be in a BUGS model (assuming
your notion of modeled data matches theirs, which
itself can present problems). We've been thinking
about that for things like DIC, or even on a data point
by point level, as in WAIC.

Doing this generically from R would be more tricky because
we're in a callback from R. I think it's actually
possible to have R call C with a function name
and arguments and have C then call back into R.

- Bob
